summary.text: The proof inductively derives a five-term block formula from the order-four recurrence and the Fibonacci recurrence: for each $k$, the values at $5k,5k+1,5k+2,5k+3,5k+4$ are respectively $(-1)^kF_{5k}$, $(-1)^kF_{5k+1}$, $(-1)^kF_{5k+1}$, $0$, and $-(-1)^kF_{5k+3}$. Splitting an arbitrary index modulo $5$ and taking absolute values then removes the signs (with $0=F_0$), yielding a Fibonacci number in every case.

full_proof.text:
Let \(F_n\) denote the Fibonacci numbers, with
\[
F_0=0,\qquad F_1=1,\qquad F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n.
\]
We consider the integer sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) defined by
\[
a_0=0,\qquad a_1=1,\qquad a_2=1,\qquad a_3=0,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=3a_{n+3}-4a_{n+2}+2a_{n+1}-a_n.
\]
We will prove that every \(|a_n|\) is a Fibonacci number.

The key fact is the following five-term pattern. For every \(k\ge 0\), put \(\varepsilon_k=(-1)^k\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{5k}   &=\varepsilon_k F_{5k},\\
a_{5k+1} &=\varepsilon_k F_{5k+1},\\
a_{5k+2} &=\varepsilon_k F_{5k+1},\\
a_{5k+3} &=0,\\
a_{5k+4} &=-\varepsilon_k F_{5k+3}.
\end{aligned} \tag{1}
\]
We prove all five identities simultaneously by induction on \(k\).

For \(k=0\), the first four identities say
\[
a_0=F_0=0,\quad a_1=F_1=1,\quad a_2=F_1=1,\quad a_3=0,
\]
which are precisely the initial conditions. The recurrence also gives
\[
a_4=3a_3-4a_2+2a_1-a_0=0-4+2-0=-2.
\]
Since \(F_3=2\), this is \(a_4=-F_3\), which is the fifth identity for \(k=0\). Thus (1) holds in the initial block.

Now suppose (1) holds for some \(k\). Write
\[
q=5k,\qquad \varepsilon=(-1)^k,
\]
and abbreviate
\[
X=F_q,\qquad Y=F_{q+1}.
\]
Repeated use of the Fibonacci recurrence gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{index}&\text{Fibonacci number in terms of }X,Y\\ \hline
q&X\\
q+1&Y\\
q+2&X+Y\\
q+3&X+2Y\\
q+4&2X+3Y\\
q+5&3X+5Y\\
q+6&5X+8Y\\
q+7&8X+13Y\\
q+8&13X+21Y.
\end{array} \tag{2}
\]
The induction hypothesis, in this notation, is
\[
a_q=\varepsilon X,\quad
a_{q+1}=\varepsilon Y,\quad
a_{q+2}=\varepsilon Y,\quad
a_{q+3}=0,\quad
a_{q+4}=-\varepsilon(X+2Y). \tag{3}
\]
We now calculate the next five terms in order from the recurrence.

First,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q+5}
 &=3a_{q+4}-4a_{q+3}+2a_{q+2}-a_{q+1}\\
 &=3[-\varepsilon(X+2Y)]-4\cdot0+2\varepsilon Y-\varepsilon Y\\
 &=-\varepsilon(3X+5Y)\\
 &=-\varepsilon F_{q+5},
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
where the last equality uses (2).

Next,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q+6}
 &=3a_{q+5}-4a_{q+4}+2a_{q+3}-a_{q+2}\\
 &=3[-\varepsilon(3X+5Y)]-4[-\varepsilon(X+2Y)]+0-\varepsilon Y\\
 &=\varepsilon(-9X-15Y+4X+8Y-Y)\\
 &=-\varepsilon(5X+8Y)\\
 &=-\varepsilon F_{q+6}.
\end{aligned} \tag{5}
\]
For the third new term,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q+7}
 &=3a_{q+6}-4a_{q+5}+2a_{q+4}-a_{q+3}\\
 &=3[-\varepsilon(5X+8Y)]-4[-\varepsilon(3X+5Y)]
      +2[-\varepsilon(X+2Y)]-0\\
 &=\varepsilon[(-15+12-2)X+(-24+20-4)Y]\\
 &=-\varepsilon(5X+8Y)\\
 &=-\varepsilon F_{q+6}.
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q+8}
 &=3a_{q+7}-4a_{q+6}+2a_{q+5}-a_{q+4}\\
 &=3[-\varepsilon F_{q+6}]-4[-\varepsilon F_{q+6}]
   +2[-\varepsilon F_{q+5}]-[-\varepsilon F_{q+3}]\\
 &=\varepsilon\bigl(F_{q+6}-2F_{q+5}+F_{q+3}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (2), the expression in parentheses is
\[
(5X+8Y)-2(3X+5Y)+(X+2Y)=0,
\]
so
\[
a_{q+8}=0. \tag{7}
\]
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q+9}
 &=3a_{q+8}-4a_{q+7}+2a_{q+6}-a_{q+5}\\
 &=0-4[-\varepsilon F_{q+6}]+2[-\varepsilon F_{q+6}]
      -[-\varepsilon F_{q+5}]\\
 &=\varepsilon(2F_{q+6}+F_{q+5}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Again by (2),
\[
2F_{q+6}+F_{q+5}
=2(5X+8Y)+(3X+5Y)
=13X+21Y
=F_{q+8}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a_{q+9}=\varepsilon F_{q+8}. \tag{8}
\]

Now \(q+5=5(k+1)\), and
\[
(-1)^{k+1}=-(-1)^k=-\varepsilon.
\]
Thus (4)–(8) can be rewritten as
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{5(k+1)}&=(-1)^{k+1}F_{5(k+1)},\\
a_{5(k+1)+1}&=(-1)^{k+1}F_{5(k+1)+1},\\
a_{5(k+1)+2}&=(-1)^{k+1}F_{5(k+1)+1},\\
a_{5(k+1)+3}&=0,\\
a_{5(k+1)+4}&=-(-1)^{k+1}F_{5(k+1)+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is exactly (1) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\), completing the induction.

It remains to deduce the desired absolute-value statement for an arbitrary index. Given \(n\ge 0\), use division by \(5\) to write uniquely
\[
n=5k+r,\qquad 0\le r<5.
\]
There are five cases.

* If \(r=0\), then by (1),
  \[
  a_n=(-1)^kF_{5k},
  \]
  and hence \(|a_n|=F_{5k}\).

* If \(r=1\), then
  \[
  a_n=(-1)^kF_{5k+1},
  \]
  so \(|a_n|=F_{5k+1}\).

* If \(r=2\), then
  \[
  a_n=(-1)^kF_{5k+1},
  \]
  and once again \(|a_n|=F_{5k+1}\). Notice that the Fibonacci index here is \(5k+1\), not necessarily \(n\).

* If \(r=3\), then \(a_n=0=F_0\), so \(|a_n|=F_0\).

* If \(r=4\), then
  \[
  a_n=-(-1)^kF_{5k+3},
  \]
  and therefore \(|a_n|=F_{5k+3}\).

These absolute-value equalities follow because \((-1)^k\), as well as its negative, has absolute value \(1\), while every Fibonacci number is nonnegative. In each residue class we have explicitly produced a nonnegative integer \(m\) for which \(|a_n|=F_m\): respectively
\[
m=5k,\quad 5k+1,\quad 5k+1,\quad 0,\quad 5k+3.
\]
Hence, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(|a_n|\) is a Fibonacci number.
